exam: A 4‑year‑old boy presents with Gower’s sign and CK 15 × ULN. What is your next diagnostic step — order MLPA to detect deletions, because it is the most common mutation type.
Explain why a male with a family history of muscular dystrophy and normal CK at age 2 still needs follow‑up — early disease may have normal CK; clinical surveillance catches later rise.
How does the genotype (out‑of‑frame vs in‑frame) predict phenotype — out‑of‑frame deletions abolish dystrophin → Duchenne; in‑frame deletions retain partial protein → Becker.
You have no access to genetic testing; how do you confirm a suspected Duchenne case — rely on clinical features, markedly elevated CK, and family pedigree; arrange referral for later testing.
Why are glucocorticoids used in Duchenne despite side effects — they improve muscle strength and delay loss of ambulation; benefits outweigh risks when monitored.
A patient with Becker dystrophy develops cardiomyopathy. What medication is indicated first — start an ACE‑inhibitor to reduce afterload and remodel the heart.
Distinguish Duchenne muscular dystrophy from spinal muscular atrophy in a low‑resource setting — DMD shows calf pseudohypertrophy and high CK; SMA has normal CK and no pseudohypertrophy.
What emergency measures are required for a Duchenne patient with acute respiratory failure — provide non‑invasive ventilation or intubation, correct hypercapnia, and monitor cardiac status.
ai.title: Dystrophin Gene and Muscular Dystrophy
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: The dystrophin gene encodes a protein that stabilises muscle cell membranes. Mutations cause Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies, presenting with progressive weakness. Understanding the genetics guides diagnosis, counselling and management in low‑resource settings.

b: Largest known human gene – prone to deletions/duplications
Critical for sarcolemma integrity during contraction
sections.p: The dystrophin gene (DMD) is the largest human gene (2.2 Mb) on Xp21.2 and produces dystrophin, a cytoskeletal protein linking the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix via the dystrophin‑glycoprotein complex (DGC).

b: Loss → membrane tears → calcium influx → necrosis
Replacement by fibrotic and fatty tissue
sections.p: Dystrophin anchors actin filaments to the DGC, which connects to laminin in the basal lamina. This protects muscle fibres from shear stress during contraction.

b: Alternative splicing can skip mutated exons (exon‑skipping therapy)
sections.p: Expression is muscle‑specific, driven by a muscle‑restricted promoter and multiple internal ribosome entry sites that allow some residual protein in milder mutations.

b: Duchenne: onset ≤5 y, rapid loss of ambulation
Becker: onset adolescence or adulthood, slower progression
sections.p: Pathogenic variants are deletions (≈65 %), duplications (≈10 %) or point mutations (≈25 %). Large deletions cause Duchenne (absent dystrophin); in‑frame deletions produce Becker (partially functional protein).

b: Ventilatory support when forced vital capacity <1 L
sections.p: Patients present with Gower’s sign, calf pseudohypertrophy and progressive weakness. Cardiac and respiratory failure are leading causes of death, often in the second‑third decade for Duchenne.

t.b: Is muscle breakdown present? Very high levels (>10 × ULN) support diagnosis; may be normal in very early disease.

t.a: Multiplex ligation‑dependent probe amplification (MLPA) or PCR
t.b: Detects deletions/duplications; first‑line genetic test when CK is elevated.
Identifies point mutations when MLPA is negative.
Assesses cardiomyopathy; start ACE‑inhibitor if ejection fraction <55 %.
Detects early respiratory decline; if unavailable, use bedside sniff test and observe nocturnal hypoventilation.

b: In low‑resource settings, rely on clinical picture + CK; send dried blood spots for genetic confirmation if possible.
Explain why steroids (prednisone, deflazacort) are first‑line for Duchenne – they delay loss of ambulation.
Distinguish Duchenne from Becker by age of onset and CK magnitude.
sections.p: Focus on inheritance pattern, genotype‑phenotype correlation, and practical steps when advanced testing is unavailable.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid decline in respiratory function (dyspnoea at rest, orthopnoea)
New onset chest pain or palpitations suggesting arrhythmia
Sudden loss of ambulation or severe contractures
